Hymn: A Mighty Fortress Is Our God
Author: Martin Luther
Story: Martin Luther wrote this battle hymn of the Reformation while plague, persecution, and political pressure closed in on the young Protestant movement. Built on Psalm 46, it confesses God himself as the fortress no enemy can take. It became the anthem of the Reformation and is still sung wherever believers face opposition.

Author: Henry Francis Lyte
Story: Henry Lyte, a pastor in the fishing town of Brixham, England, wrote this hymn as tuberculosis was ending his life. On his final Sunday in the pulpit, knowing he would soon leave for Italy in a last hope of recovery, he gave his congregation this evening prayer. He died weeks later in Nice, France. It has been sung at bedsides, funerals, and farewells ever since.

Hymn: All Hail the Power of Jesus' Name
Author: Edward Perronet
Story: Edward Perronet, a friend and fellow worker of John and Charles Wesley, wrote this hymn of Christ's kingship in 1779. Its call to crown him Lord of all has made it a coronation hymn of the church, sung at missionary farewells, revivals, and great gatherings for more than two centuries.

Author: John Newton
Story: John Newton once captained slave ships. In a violent storm off Ireland in 1748 he cried out to God, and his slow conversion began. Years later, as a pastor in Olney, England, he wrote this testimony of grace that found a wretch and made him new. Near the end of his life he worked alongside William Wilberforce for the abolition of the slave trade he had once served.

Author: Irish, 8th century; translated by Mary Byrne
Story: This prayer comes from early medieval Ireland, traditionally linked to the poet Dallan Forgaill in the 8th century. It asks God to be the believer's sight, wisdom, and treasure above all else. Mary Byrne translated the old Irish text into English in 1905, and Eleanor Hull versified it in 1912, giving the church one of its most beloved prayers of devotion.

Author: Fanny Crosby
Story: Fanny Crosby, blind from infancy, wrote more than 8,000 hymns. In 1873 her friend Phoebe Knapp played a new tune for her and asked what it said. Crosby answered at once with the words of this hymn: a song of quiet certainty that Jesus is ours and heaven is ahead. It remains one of the most sung testimonies of assurance in the church.

Hymn: Come Thou Fount of Every Blessing
Author: Robert Robinson
Story: Robert Robinson was converted at age 22 under George Whitefield's preaching and wrote this hymn three years later. Its image of the Ebenezer stone comes from 1 Samuel 7, where Samuel raised a stone and said, 'Thus far the Lord has helped us.' The honest line about a heart prone to wander has kept the hymn close to believers who know their own need of grace.

Author: Matthew Bridges
Story: Matthew Bridges, an English writer who converted from Anglicanism to Catholicism, wrote this hymn of Christ's many crowns in 1851. Godfrey Thring later added verses, and together the hymn crowns Jesus as Lord of life, love, and heaven itself. Its tune, Diademata, was written by George Elvey for a missionary anniversary.

Author: Thomas Chisholm
Story: Thomas Chisholm lived a quiet life of frail health and modest means, never wealthy and often unwell. Out of that ordinary life he wrote this hymn on Lamentations 3: new mercies every morning, faithfulness without end. William Runyan set it to music in 1923, and it became beloved through the Moody Bible Institute and Billy Graham's crusades.

Hymn: Guide Me, O Thou Great Jehovah
Author: William Williams
Story: William Williams, the great Welsh evangelist, wrote this hymn in Welsh in 1745 as a pilgrim's prayer for the wilderness journey. Peter Williams translated it into English, and the towering Welsh tune Cwm Rhondda carried it around the world. It pictures the Christian life as Israel's journey: led by cloud and fire, fed with heavenly bread, brought safely home.

Author: Reginald Heber
Story: Reginald Heber, later Bishop of Calcutta, wrote this hymn for Trinity Sunday in 1826. It takes its words from the worship of heaven in Revelation 4 and Isaiah 6, where angels cry holy to the three-in-one God. The tune Nicaea, named for the council that defended the Trinity, was written by John Bacchus Dykes.

Author: Unknown (signed 'K')
Story: This hymn appeared in John Rippon's Selection of Hymns in 1787, signed only with the letter K, so its author remains unknown. Each verse speaks a promise of God directly to the fearful believer: fear not, I am with you; when you pass through the waters, I will be with you. It was a favorite of American presidents and soldiers alike.

Author: Carl Boberg; English adaptation by Stuart Hine
Story: Swedish pastor Carl Boberg wrote the original poem in 1885 after a thunderstorm broke over the Swedish countryside and church bells rang out across the valley. Missionary Stuart Hine later adapted it into English, adding verses shaped by his own years in Ukraine. Billy Graham's crusades carried it around the world, and it became one of the most sung hymns of the twentieth century.

Author: Albert Brumley
Story: Albert Brumley wrote this joyful song about heaven in 1929 while picking cotton on his family's farm in Oklahoma. It pictures the believer's release from earthly trouble into glory. It became one of the most recorded songs in gospel music and a staple of funerals, revivals, and family singings across America.

Author: Annie Hawks
Story: Annie Hawks, a Brooklyn wife and mother, wrote this hymn in 1872 after a morning of ordinary household cares left her feeling how constantly she needed Christ. Her pastor, Robert Lowry, composed the tune and added the refrain. It is a plain, honest prayer that dependence on Jesus is not for crises only, but for every hour.

Author: Keith Getty and Stuart Townend
Story: Keith Getty and Stuart Townend wrote this modern hymn in 2001 with a deliberate aim: to confess the whole gospel in a single song, from incarnation to resurrection, so a congregation could sing its faith complete. It spread rapidly through churches worldwide and became one of the defining hymns of the twenty-first century church.

Hymn: It Is Well with My Soul
Author: Horatio Spafford
Story: Horatio Spafford, a Chicago lawyer, lost his fortune in the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. Two years later he sent his wife and four daughters ahead to Europe by ship; the vessel collided mid-Atlantic and all four girls drowned. Sailing to join his grieving wife, Spafford passed over the spot where they were lost and wrote this hymn of peace that does not depend on circumstances.

Author: Elvina Hall
Story: Elvina Hall, a member of a Methodist church in Baltimore, wrote these words in 1865 during a Sunday service while the choir sang another hymn. She scribbled the lines in her hymnal, and the church organist, John Grape, realized he had a tune written years earlier that fit them exactly. The pairing has carried this song of full atonement ever since.

Author: Charlotte Elliott
Story: Charlotte Elliott, an invalid sister of a London clergyman, was distressed that her illness kept her from doing anything useful for God. A visiting minister told her to come to Christ just as she was. Years later, on the anniversary of that conversation, she wrote this invitation hymn. Billy Graham's crusades made it the most famous altar-call hymn in the world.

Author: Charles Wesley
Story: Charles Wesley wrote this great hymn of divine love in 1747. It asks for the love of God to dwell fully in the believer's heart, making the Christian life complete. Set to the tune Beecher by John Zundel, it has been sung at weddings, revivals, and state occasions, and is often called Wesley's finest hymn.

Hymn: My Hope Is Built on Nothing Less
Author: Edward Mote
Story: Edward Mote, a London cabinetmaker who became a Baptist pastor, wrote the refrain of this hymn first as his daily motto: on Christ the solid Rock I stand. The full hymn grew from it, contrasting every sinking sand of human hope with the one foundation that holds. It is still sung wherever believers need to remember what their hope rests on.

Author: Sarah Flower Adams
Story: Sarah Flower Adams wrote this hymn in 1841 for her brother-in-law, a minister preaching on Jacob's dream of a ladder reaching to heaven. Its prayer to be drawn nearer to God through every circumstance made it beloved at funerals and farewells. Tradition holds that the band of the Titanic played it as the ship went down.

Hymn: O for a Thousand Tongues to Sing
Author: Charles Wesley
Story: Charles Wesley wrote this hymn in 1739 on the first anniversary of his conversion, when his heart was, in his own words, strangely warmed. Originally eighteen verses, it pours out praise for the grace that saved him. It has opened Methodist worship and revival meetings for nearly three centuries.

Hymn: Pass Me Not, O Gentle Savior
Author: Fanny Crosby
Story: Fanny Crosby wrote this hymn in 1868 after speaking at a prison service, where a young inmate cried out, 'Good Lord, do not pass me by.' The plea of the blind beggar Bartimaeus in Luke 18 stands behind it. William Doane set it to music, and it became one of the great invitation hymns of the revival era.

Author: Augustus Toplady
Story: Augustus Toplady wrote this hymn in 1776, drawing on the picture of Moses sheltered in the cleft of the rock in Exodus 33. Tradition says Toplady himself sheltered from a storm in a cleft rock at Burrington Combe in England, though the story is debated. Either way, the hymn's prayer to hide in Christ's wounds has comforted believers for nearly 250 years.

Author: Will L. Thompson
Story: Will Thompson, an Ohio music publisher and evangelist, wrote this invitation hymn in 1880. Its gentle call to come home became a favorite of Dwight Moody and Ira Sankey's great evangelistic campaigns. It is still sung at altar calls and funerals, inviting the weary to answer Jesus.

Author: Russell Carter
Story: Russell Carter, a Pennsylvania preacher and teacher, wrote this hymn in 1886 while recovering from a serious heart condition. Unable to continue his usual work, he rested his faith on God's promises and turned that experience into a marching song of assurance. It became a staple of Sunday schools and revivals.

Hymn: Take My Life and Let It Be
Author: Frances Ridley Havergal
Story: Frances Ridley Havergal wrote this hymn of consecration in 1874 during a visit to friends, when she felt freshly convicted to give every part of her life to God. Verse by verse it offers hands, feet, voice, silver, gold, will, and heart. It remains the church's classic prayer of total surrender.

Author: George Bennard
Story: George Bennard, a Methodist evangelist, wrote this hymn in 1913 during revival meetings in Albion, Michigan. He had been teased about the meaning of the cross and spent weeks meditating on it before the song came. It became the most popular gospel song of its generation and is still sung wherever the cross is preached.

Author: John Sammis
Story: John Sammis wrote this hymn in 1887 after hearing Dwight Moody preach on obedience, and Daniel Towner composed its tune. Its simple message, that there is no other way to be happy in Jesus but to trust and obey, made it a favorite of Sunday schools, camps, and missionary gatherings.

Hymn: What a Friend We Have in Jesus
Author: Joseph Scriven
Story: Joseph Scriven, an Irish immigrant to Canada, wrote this hymn in 1855 to comfort his sick mother back in Ireland. Scriven had lost two fiancees to death, gave away his wealth, and spent his life serving the poor. He never meant the poem for publication, but it became one of the most beloved hymns of prayer ever written.

Hymn: When I Survey the Wondrous Cross
Author: Isaac Watts
Story: Isaac Watts, often called the father of English hymnody, wrote this hymn in 1707 when he was 33. Breaking from strict psalm paraphrases, he dared to write freely of Christ's cross, and the church has counted it among the greatest hymns in the language ever since. It turns the gaze from human pride to the crucified Savior.

Author: Ada R. Habershon; music by Charles H. Gabriel
Story: Ada Habershon wrote this funeral hymn in 1907 about the hope that death does not break the family circle, because heaven reunites those who die in the Lord. Charles Gabriel set it to music, and it later became a beloved standard of gospel and country music, sung at countless funerals and family gatherings.

Author: Matt Redman and Jonas Myrin
Story: Matt Redman co-wrote this song with Jonas Myrin in 2011, basing it on Psalm 103's call to bless the Lord and forget none of his benefits. Also known under the alternate title Bless the Lord, O My Soul, it won the Grammy Award for Best Contemporary Christian Music Song in 2013 and became a staple of congregational praise.

Hymn: A Charge to Keep I Have
Author: Charles Wesley
Story: Charles Wesley first published this hymn in 1762 in his Short Hymns on Select Passages of the Holy Scriptures, where it was based on Leviticus 8:35. It treats the Christian life as a stewardship to be kept faithfully from youth to old age, with an account to give at the end. It is most commonly sung to the tune BOYLSTON by Lowell Mason.

Author: Johann Heermann
Story: Johann Heermann, a Lutheran pastor in Silesia, wrote this Passion hymn in 1630 during the miseries of the Thirty Years' War, asking why the innocent Jesus suffered and answering that it was for the singer's own sin. Robert Bridges' English translation is the best known. It is sung in Lent and Holy Week as a penitential meditation on the cross.

Hymn: Alas! and Did My Saviour Bleed
Author: Isaac Watts
Story: Isaac Watts published this hymn in 1707 in Hymns and Spiritual Songs. It meditates with astonishment that Christ would suffer and die for sinners, and it closes with the believer's resolve to give all to him in return. It is often sung to the tune MARTYRDOM.

Author: Francis of Assisi
Hymn: All Creatures of Our God and King
Story: Francis of Assisi wrote the Canticle of the Sun in 1225, near the end of his life, praising God through sun, moon, wind, water, fire, and earth. William Henry Draper turned it into this English hymn in 1919, keeping its call for all creation to praise its Maker. It remains one of the most widely sung hymns of creation praise.

Author: Theodulph of Orléans
Story: Theodulph, bishop of Orléans, is traditionally said to have written this Palm Sunday hymn around 820, possibly while imprisoned after falling from political favor; that imprisonment story is tradition, not certain fact. Its refrain echoes the crowd's welcome of Jesus into Jerusalem. Catherine Winkworth's English translation brought it into wide English use in the 1850s.
Themes: Palm Sunday; Worship; Kingship of Christ

Hymn: All the Way My Savior Leads Me
Author: Fanny J. Crosby
Story: Fanny Crosby wrote this hymn in 1875, and it was her first text set to music by Robert Lowry, who composed the tune specially for the words. It was first published in 1875 in Brightest and Best, edited by Lowry and William Howard Doane. Crosby later linked the hymn to an answered prayer for a small sum of money she urgently needed, which she took as an instance of God's guidance.

Hymn: Am I a Soldier of the Cross
Author: Isaac Watts
Story: Isaac Watts published this hymn in 1724 in Hymns and Spiritual Songs. It asks whether the believer will shrink from the hardships of following Christ or follow him boldly, even at cost. It is commonly sung to the tune ARLINGTON.

Hymn: And Can It Be That I Should Gain
Author: Charles Wesley
Story: Charles Wesley wrote this hymn in May 1738, shortly after his evangelical conversion, and it first appeared in Hymns and Sacred Poems in 1739. It marvels that Christ would die for one who had opposed him, and it has become one of the most loved testimonies of personal redemption in English hymnody. Its best-known tune is SAGINA, composed by Thomas Campbell.

Author: Charles Wesley
Story: Charles Wesley first published this hymn in Hymns and Sacred Poems in 1742 under the title Behold the Man. It presents Christ as the believer's surety before God's throne, interceding on the basis of his wounds, and it urges the guilty soul to shake off fear. It is widely sung to the tune LENOX by Lewis Edson.

Author: Bill Gaither and Gloria Gaither
Story: Bill and Gloria Gaither wrote this song in 1971 as they awaited the birth of their third child in troubled times, finding confidence for the future in the risen Christ. Its assurance that life is worth living because Jesus lives made it one of the best-known gospel songs of the twentieth century.

Author: Matt Redman and Beth Redman
Story: Matt and Beth Redman wrote this song in 2002, releasing it on the album Where Angels Fear to Tread. Following Job's example, it blesses God's name in times of plenty and in times of want, and it became one of the defining worship songs of the early 2000s.

Hymn: Blest Be the Tie That Binds
Author: John Fawcett
Story: John Fawcett published this hymn in 1782 under the title Brotherly Love. It celebrates the bond of Christian fellowship that unites believers in shared sorrows, prayers, and hopes. The widely repeated story that Fawcett wrote it when deciding to stay with his poor congregation rather than accept a London pulpit is traditional and lacks direct evidence, so it is not stated here as fact. It is commonly sung to the tune DENNIS.

Author: Keith Getty, Kristyn Getty and Stuart Townend
Story: Keith Getty, Kristyn Getty, and Stuart Townend wrote this hymn in 2009, copyrighted that year by Thankyou Music. Following the pattern of Hebrews 11, it moves from creation and the patriarchs through the prophets to the church's mission, calling believers to walk by faith and not by sight.

Author: Traditional
Hymn: Christ Is Made the Sure Foundation
Story: This hymn comes from a seventh-century Latin hymn, Urbs beata Jerusalem, sung at the dedication of a church, picturing the church as a city built on Christ the cornerstone. John Mason Neale translated it into English in the nineteenth century. It is still sung at church dedications and anniversaries, and whenever the church confesses Christ as its foundation.

Author: Martin Luther
Story: Martin Luther wrote this Easter hymn in 1524, reworking an older German Easter song into a Reformation confession of Christ's victory over death and sin. It pictures Christ as the Passover Lamb whose death breaks death's bonds and opens life to believers. It has remained a classic Lutheran Easter hymn ever since.

Hymn: Christ the Lord Is Risen Today
Author: Charles Wesley
Story: Charles Wesley wrote this Easter hymn in 1739 for use at the first service in the Foundry, the early Methodist meeting place in London. Its repeated alleluias celebrate Christ's resurrection as the defeat of death and the ground of Christian hope. It is traditionally sung to the tune EASTER HYMN.

Author: Traditional
Hymn: Come, Holy Ghost, Our Souls Inspire
Story: This hymn is the English form of the ninth-century Latin Veni Creator Spiritus, traditionally attributed to Rabanus Maurus, though that attribution is not certain. It was sung at ordinations, the opening of councils, and other solemn occasions as a prayer for the Spirit's guidance. John Cosin's 1627 translation is the best-known English version; another well-known translation begins Come, Holy Ghost, Creator Blest.

Author: Charles Wesley
Story: Charles Wesley wrote this Advent hymn in 1744, and it appeared in Hymns for the Nativity of Our Lord in 1745. It was written to express Israel's longing for the promised Messiah and the church's longing for his return. It is commonly sung to the Welsh tune HYFRYDOL.

Hymn: Come, We That Love the Lord
Author: Isaac Watts
Story: Isaac Watts published this hymn in 1707 in Hymns and Spiritual Songs. It invites all who love the Lord to join in joyful praise as pilgrims journeying together toward heaven, and it is also known by the alternate title We're Marching to Zion, taken from its later refrain. It is commonly sung to the tune MARCHING TO ZION.

Hymn: Come, Ye Sinners, Poor and Needy
Author: Joseph Hart
Story: Joseph Hart first published this hymn in 1759, originally under the title Come, and Welcome to Jesus Christ. Written after Hart's conversion under George Whitefield's preaching, it invites sinners, the weary, and the heavy-laden to come to Jesus just as they are. It is commonly sung to the tune RESTORATION, an American folk melody.

Author: Martin Luther
Hymn: Dear Christians, One and All, Rejoice
Story: Martin Luther wrote this hymn in 1523, one of his earliest hymns, telling in song how God in mercy sent his Son to rescue lost sinners who could not save themselves. It became a kind of sung summary of justification by faith for the young Reformation churches. Its tune, Nun freut euch, was one of the first Lutheran chorale tunes.

Author: William Whiting
Story: William Whiting, headmaster of the Winchester College Choristers' School, wrote this hymn in 1860 to comfort a pupil who was anxious about an approaching sea voyage. It was first published, with revisions, in Hymns Ancient and Modern in 1861. John Bacchus Dykes composed the tune Melita in 1861, named for Malta, where Paul was shipwrecked, and the hymn became widely known as the Navy Hymn.

Author: William Walsham How
Story: William Walsham How wrote the words in 1864 for All Saints' Day, celebrating the faithful of every generation. The best-known tune, Sine Nomine, was not composed until 1906, when Ralph Vaughan Williams wrote it for the English Hymnal. The hymn moves from the saints who have finished their course to believers still running, and ends with the vision of the heavenly multitude.

Author: Martin Luther
Hymn: From Heaven Above to Earth I Come
Story: Martin Luther wrote this Christmas hymn in 1535, casting it as the angels' announcement to the shepherds and a child's joyful answer. Tradition holds that he wrote it for his own family's Christmas celebration, though that detail is not firmly documented. It retells the Bethlehem story in simple verses that children and congregations could sing together.

Hymn: Glorious Things of Thee Are Spoken
Author: John Newton
Story: John Newton published this hymn in the Olney Hymns of 1779, written on Isaiah 33:20-21 with echoes of Psalm 87. It celebrates Zion, the city of God, as a picture of the church: founded on Christ, fed by streams of grace, and kept safe by God's presence. It is most commonly sung to the tune AUSTRIAN HYMN by Joseph Haydn.

Hymn: God Moves in a Mysterious Way
Author: William Cowper
Story: William Cowper wrote this hymn in 1773, and it was first published in 1774 in John Newton's Twenty-six Letters on Religious Subjects, before appearing in the Olney Hymns of 1779. Written during a period of severe depression, it confesses trust in God's wise providence even when his purposes cannot be understood. It is most frequently sung to the tune DUNDEE. The popular story linking it to a prevented suicide attempt is traditional and not firmly documented, so it is not stated here as fact.

Author: Traditional
Story: This Christmas hymn grew from the fourteenth-century Latin-German carol In dulci jubilo, which mixes Latin and German lines in joyful praise of the newborn Christ. Its exact author is unknown. John Mason Neale's English version, published in the nineteenth century, made it a standard English Christmas carol.

Author: Philip P. Bliss
Story: This hymn is also known under the title Man of Sorrows. Philip Bliss wrote both words and tune, and it was first published in 1875 in the International Lessons Monthly under the title Redemption, then included in Gospel Hymns No. 2 in 1876. It follows Isaiah's suffering servant through Christ's atoning death to his exaltation, with each stanza closing in praise of so great a Saviour.

Author: Charles Wesley
Story: Charles Wesley wrote this Christmas hymn in 1739, a year after his conversion, and it was first published in Hymns and Sacred Poems. It announces the birth of Christ as good news of peace between God and humanity, drawing on the angels' announcement to the shepherds. The familiar tune MENDELSSOHN, adapted from Felix Mendelssohn, became attached to the text in the mid-nineteenth century.

Author: Fanny J. Crosby
Story: Fanny Crosby wrote this hymn in 1890 to fit a tune already composed by William James Kirkpatrick, her usual practice of writing words to a given melody. It first appeared in Finest of the Wheat, No. 1, in 1890. Its image of shelter in the cleft of the rock echoes Moses being sheltered by God, and the hymn presents Christ as refuge and redeemer in trial.

Author: Dan Schutte
Story: Dan Schutte, a Jesuit composer, wrote this song in 1981 while at Saint Louis University, basing it on Isaiah's call in Isaiah 6 and Samuel's answer in 1 Samuel 3. Written for ordinations and commissioning services, it spread far beyond its Catholic origins and is now sung across denominations.

Author: Tim Hughes
Story: Tim Hughes, a young worship leader in England, wrote this song in 2000, also known by its opening phrase Light of the World. It moves from Christ's humble coming to the worship he deserves, and it became one of the most widely used contemporary worship songs of the 2000s.

Author: Civilla D. Martin
Hymn: His Eye Is on the Sparrow
Story: Civilla Martin wrote the words of this hymn in 1905, with music by Charles H. Gabriel. According to Martin's own account, the central phrase came from a bedridden friend who, despite her suffering, spoke of God's care for the smallest bird, and Martin carried the thought home into this song of trust.

Author: Matt Boswell and Matt Papa
Story: Matt Boswell and Matt Papa wrote this modern hymn in 2016, setting God's mercy above the weight of human sin. Drawing on Psalm 103's picture of mercy as high as the heavens are above the earth, it has become a staple of contemporary congregational singing about forgiveness.

Author: Stuart Townend
Hymn: How Deep the Father's Love for Us
Story: Stuart Townend wrote this hymn in England, with a stated copyright date of 1995; its first recorded appearance came on a live Stoneleigh Bible Week album in 1996. Townend aimed for a modern hymn with the humble gratitude of an older hymn, dwelling on the Father giving his only Son to make sinners his treasure.

Author: Chris Tomlin, Jesse Reeves and Ed Cash
Story: Chris Tomlin wrote this worship song with Jesse Reeves and Ed Cash, releasing it on his 2004 album Arriving. Built on the greatness of God above all names, it became one of the most widely sung contemporary worship songs in the world and is now sung in many languages.

Hymn: How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds
Author: John Newton
Story: John Newton published this hymn in the Olney Hymns of 1779. It praises the name of Jesus as comfort to the sorrowful, rest to the weary, and the believer's rock and shield. It is often sung to the tune ST PETER by Alexander Reinagle.

Hymn: I Sing the Mighty Power of God
Author: Isaac Watts
Story: Isaac Watts published this hymn in 1715 in his Divine Songs for children, though it has long been sung by adults as well. It praises God's power and wisdom displayed in creation, from the seas and mountains to the smallest creatures. The tune ELLACOMBE is its most common setting.

Author: C. Austin Miles
Story: C. Austin Miles, a pharmacist turned hymnwriter, wrote both the words and music of this gospel song in 1912. It pictures Mary Magdalene meeting the risen Christ in the garden on Easter morning, and it became one of the most beloved gospel songs of the twentieth century.

Author: Andrew Peterson
Story: Andrew Peterson wrote this song in 2018 for his album Resurrection Letters, Vol. 1. Structured as a call and response drawn from Revelation 5, it asks who is worthy to open the scroll and answers with the praise of the Lamb who was slain.

Hymn: It Came Upon the Midnight Clear
Author: Edmund Hamilton Sears
Story: Edmund Hamilton Sears, a Unitarian minister in Massachusetts, wrote this carol in 1849, in a period of social tension in America and unrest in Europe. Richard Storrs Willis composed the tune Carol for it in 1850. Unlike many carols, it dwells on the angels' message of peace in a weary world and on the hope that the message will one day be fully heard.

Author: Bernard of Cluny
Story: Bernard, a twelfth-century monk of Cluny, wrote a long Latin poem contrasting the sorrows of this world with the glory of the heavenly Jerusalem. John Mason Neale translated the heavenward portion in the nineteenth century, and this hymn is drawn from that translation. It sings of the city where sorrow ends and God's people see him face to face.

Hymn: Jesus, Keep Me Near the Cross
Author: Fanny J. Crosby
Story: This hymn is also known by the alternate titles Near the Cross and In the Cross. William Howard Doane composed the tune first and gave it to Fanny Crosby, who supplied the text in 1869. It first appeared that year in Bright Jewels, a Sunday school collection compiled by Bradbury, Doane, and others. The hymn keeps the cross at the centre of daily Christian life, looking beyond present life to rest in heaven.

Author: Charles Wesley
Story: Charles Wesley wrote this hymn in 1740, and it appeared in Hymns and Sacred Poems that same year. It pictures the believer fleeing to Christ for refuge and shelter, like a traveler seeking cover in a storm. It is often counted among Wesley's finest hymns and is widely sung to the Welsh tune ABERYSTWYTH.

Author: Anna B. Warner
Story: Anna Warner wrote this text in 1860 as part of her novel Say and Seal, where it was spoken to comfort a dying child in the story. William Bradbury composed the tune Jesus Loves Me and added the familiar refrain in 1862. Originally a children's song, it became one of the most widely translated and sung Christian songs in the world.

Hymn: Jesus Shall Reign Where'er the Sun
Author: Isaac Watts
Story: Isaac Watts published this hymn in 1719 in his Psalms of David Imitated, as a paraphrase of Psalm 72. It looks forward to the worldwide reign of Christ, with people of every nation blessing his name. It is commonly sung to the tune DUKE STREET and became a favorite missionary hymn.

Author: Bernard of Clairvaux
Hymn: Jesus, the Very Thought of Thee
Story: This hymn is drawn from a long Latin poem on the name of Jesus traditionally attributed to Bernard of Clairvaux, the twelfth-century Cistercian abbot, though the full poem's authorship is not certain. Edward Caswall's nineteenth-century translation gives the best-known English verses. It meditates on the sweetness of Jesus' name and presence to the believing heart.

Author: Isaac Watts
Story: Isaac Watts published this hymn in 1719 in his Psalms of David Imitated, as a paraphrase of Psalm 98 looking forward to the reign of Christ. Although now sung at Christmas, it celebrates Christ's kingship over all the earth rather than his birth alone. The tune ANTIOCH, adapted by Lowell Mason, became its standard setting in the nineteenth century.

Author: Brooke Ligertwood, Scott Ligertwood and Jason Ingram
Story: Brooke Ligertwood, Scott Ligertwood, and Jason Ingram wrote this hymn for Hillsong Worship in 2019, releasing it on the album Awake. In four verses it traces the whole gospel story, from creation and the fall through the incarnation, cross, and resurrection to the church and the return of Christ.

Author: John Henry Newman
Story: John Henry Newman wrote this poem, originally titled The Pillar of the Cloud, in 1833 while becalmed in the Straits of Bonifacio on his way home from Italy, after illness had delayed his journey. It was first published in the British Magazine in 1834. John Bacchus Dykes later composed the tune Lux Benigna for it in 1865, though it is also sung to Sandon.

Author: Elisha A. Hoffman
Story: Elisha Hoffman wrote the words in 1887, and Anthony Showalter composed the tune Showalter the same year. The hymn grew out of a correspondence between the two men about the support believers find in God, and it was published in a gospel song collection of the period. Its refrain image of leaning on everlasting arms has made it a favourite at funerals, revivals, and times of weakness.

Author: Traditional
Hymn: Let All Mortal Flesh Keep Silence
Story: This hymn comes from the Liturgy of St. James, one of the oldest Christian liturgies, where it was sung as the bread and wine were brought forward. Its call to reverent silence before Christ's presence reflects the awe of that moment in worship. Gerard Moultrie's 1864 English translation, set to the French carol tune Picardy, brought it into English hymnals.

Hymn: Lo! He Comes with Clouds Descending
Author: John Cennick; Charles Wesley
Story: This hymn began as an Advent hymn by John Cennick, published in his Collection of Sacred Hymns in 1752, and Charles Wesley substantially rewrote it for Hymns of Intercession for All Mankind in 1758. It pictures the return of Christ in glory, when every eye will see him. It is most commonly sung to the tune HELMSLEY.

Author: Martin Luther
Hymn: Lord, Keep Us Steadfast in Your Word
Story: Martin Luther wrote this short prayer hymn in 1543, asking God to keep his people steadfast in the Word and to restrain the enemies of the gospel. It was written for children to sing as a prayer for the church under threat, and it became a regular prayer hymn in Lutheran worship. Its plain petition still fits any congregation asking to hold fast to Scripture.

Author: Ben Fielding and Reuben Morgan
Story: Ben Fielding and Reuben Morgan of Hillsong Worship wrote this song in 2006, releasing it on the album of the same name. It proclaims God as the Saviour who rescues all who call on his name, and it became one of Hillsong's most widely sung songs worldwide.

Author: Eleanor Farjeon
Story: Eleanor Farjeon wrote these words in 1931 for the Scottish Gaelic melody Bunessan, praising God for the new morning as part of the fresh creation. It reached a vast new audience when Cat Stevens recorded it in 1971, and it has remained a beloved morning hymn ever since.

Author: William R. Featherston
Story: William Featherston, a teenager in Montreal, wrote this poem about love for Christ, dated by some sources to 1862; it was first published anonymously in the London Hymn Book in 1864. The author's identity was only established decades later, after his early death. Adoniram Judson Gordon, dissatisfied with the earlier setting, composed the tune Gordon for it, published in 1876, and that pairing became standard.

Author: Robert Lowry
Story: Robert Lowry wrote both words and tune in 1876, asking in each stanza what can wash away sin and answering with the blood of Christ alone. It was published in gospel song collections of the Moody and Sankey era and became a standard evangelistic hymn. The hymn draws directly on the New Testament teaching that forgiveness comes through Christ's shed blood.

Author: Martin Rinkart
Hymn: Now Thank We All Our God
Story: Martin Rinkart, pastor at Eilenburg during the Thirty Years' War, wrote this thanksgiving hymn around 1636, a year when plague and war had devastated his town and he had buried thousands, including members of his own family. That it is a song of thanks written in such suffering is what has made it endure. It is sung at harvest, at year's end, and in national thanksgivings.

Author: Traditional
Story: This Advent hymn grew out of the ancient Latin O Antiphons, short chants sung in the days before Christmas that address Christ by Old Testament titles such as Emmanuel and Dayspring. The exact date and author of the hymn form are unknown, and the Latin verses were later combined into one hymn. John Mason Neale's 1851 English translation made it a standard Advent hymn in English.

Hymn: O for a Closer Walk with God
Author: William Cowper
Story: William Cowper wrote this hymn in 1772, and it appeared in the Olney Hymns of 1779, the collection he produced with John Newton. It laments the loss of the closeness with God the believer once knew and prays for the return of the Holy Spirit's restoring presence. It is commonly sung to the tune CAITHNESS.

Author: Phillips Brooks
Story: Phillips Brooks wrote this carol in 1868 for the children of his Philadelphia Sunday school, three years after he had visited Bethlehem on Christmas Eve. His organist, Lewis Redner, composed the tune St Louis for it the same year. The carol contrasts the quiet of the small town with the birth of Christ within it, and it remains one of the most sung American Christmas hymns.

Author: Philipp Nicolai
Hymn: O Morning Star, How Fair and Bright
Story: Philipp Nicolai wrote this hymn in 1599, the same year as Wake, Awake, for Night Is Flying, as a song of love and praise to Christ the Morning Star. Written amid the same plague year in Unna, it turns from suffering to adoration of the Bridegroom who brings light and life. It is often called the queen of chorales, paired with Nicolai's king of chorales.

Author: Paul Gerhardt
Story: This Passion hymn began as a Latin poem on Christ's suffering, traditionally attributed to Arnulf of Louvain in the thirteenth century, though that attribution is not certain. Paul Gerhardt turned it into German in 1656, and James Waddell Alexander's English translation made it widely known. It meditates verse by verse on the wounded head of Christ on the cross, and is sung above all in Holy Week.

Author: Jean Tisserand
Hymn: O Sons and Daughters, Let Us Sing
Story: Jean Tisserand, a fifteenth-century French Franciscan, wrote this Easter hymn retelling the resurrection appearances, from the empty tomb to the disciples' joy and Thomas's confession. Its repeated alleluias carry the Easter proclamation from verse to verse. John Mason Neale's English translation brought it into English Easter worship.

Author: Aurelius Prudentius
Story: The Latin poet Aurelius Prudentius wrote this hymn of Christ's eternal sonship in the late fourth or early fifth century, as part of a longer poem for the hours of the day. It confesses that the Son, begotten before the world began, was born of Mary yet remains God. John Mason Neale's translation and the medieval chant tune Divinum Mysterium carry it in English hymnals; it is also known by the alternate title Of the Father's Heart Begotten.

Author: Sabine Baring-Gould
Story: Sabine Baring-Gould, an Anglican clergyman, wrote this hymn in 1865 for a children's procession between two Yorkshire villages, originally as a marching song for young people. Arthur Sullivan composed the tune St Gertrude for it in 1871, and the pairing made it one of the best-known Victorian marching hymns. Its military imagery describes the church advancing in spiritual conflict, not earthly warfare.

Hymn: Our God, Our Help in Ages Past
Author: Isaac Watts
Story: Isaac Watts published this hymn in 1719 in his Psalms of David Imitated, as a paraphrase of Psalm 90. It contrasts human frailty and the brevity of life with God's everlasting faithfulness across generations. It is traditionally sung to the tune ST ANNE and is often chosen at funerals, remembrances, and national occasions.

Author: Martin Luther
Hymn: Out of the Depths I Cry to You
Story: Martin Luther's 1524 paraphrase of Psalm 130 turns the psalmist's cry from the depths into a Reformation prayer: sinners plead for mercy, confess that no works can earn forgiveness, and wait on God's gracious word. It was one of the earliest Lutheran psalm hymns and was sung at funerals as well as in ordinary worship. Its tune, Aus tiefer Not, is one of Luther's own chorale melodies.

Hymn: Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven
Author: Henry Francis Lyte
Story: Henry Francis Lyte wrote this paraphrase of Psalm 103 in 1834 for his congregation at Lower Brixham in Devon, where he ministered to a fishing community. It was published that year in his Spirit of the Psalms. John Goss composed the tune Lauda Anima for it in 1869, and the hymn became one of the great English hymns of praise.

Author: Joachim Neander
Hymn: Praise to the Lord, the Almighty
Story: Joachim Neander, a young Reformed pastor and teacher in seventeenth-century Germany, wrote this paraphrase of Psalm 103 in 1680. Neander loved to walk and worship in the valley near Düsseldorf that later bore his name, the Neanderthal, and his hymns breathe that delight in God's creation and care. Catherine Winkworth's translation made it one of the great English praise hymns.

Author: Thomas A. Dorsey
Story: Thomas A. Dorsey, known as the father of gospel music, wrote this song in 1932 in grief after his wife and newborn son died. A prayer for God to lead through darkness, it became an anthem of comfort and was sung at the funeral of Martin Luther King Jr. in 1968.

Author: Charles Wesley
Story: Charles Wesley wrote this hymn in 1744 and published it in Hymns for Our Lord's Resurrection in 1746. It calls God's people to rejoice because Christ reigns as King, even while his kingdom is not yet fully seen. The tune DARWALL, by John Darwall, is its most common setting.

Author: Fanny J. Crosby
Story: Composer William Howard Doane gave Fanny Crosby the subject of rescuing the perishing, and she wrote the text in 1869 after speaking at a New York City mission in the Bowery. That evening a young man who had drifted from his mother's teaching came forward for prayer and professed faith. Crosby completed the hymn that night, and Doane set it to music; it later became a staple of Moody and Sankey evangelistic meetings.

Author: Jennie Lee Riddle
Story: Jennie Lee Riddle wrote this song in 2004, drawing on the heavenly worship scenes of Revelation 4 and 5. Popularized in recordings by Kari Jobe and Gateway Worship, it carries the praise of the living creatures and elders into congregational singing.

Author: Paul Speratus
Story: Paul Speratus, a supporter of Luther, wrote this hymn in 1523, the same year as Luther's earliest hymns, setting out the Reformation teaching that salvation comes by grace through faith, not by works of the law. It was published in the first Lutheran hymnbooks and became one of the Reformation's defining songs. Its plain, doctrinal verses made it a teaching hymn for new congregations.

Author: Ambrose of Milan
Story: This Advent hymn began as the Latin Veni, redemptor gentium by Ambrose, bishop of Milan in the fourth century, confessing Christ's miraculous birth as true God and true man. Martin Luther made a German version of it in 1524, which is why it is closely tied to the Reformation as well as to the early church. It is sung at Advent as a call for the promised Savior to come.

Hymn: Shall We Gather at the River
Author: Robert Lowry
Story: Robert Lowry, a Baptist minister and hymn writer, wrote both words and tune in 1864 during the American Civil War, and it was first published in 1865. The river in the hymn is the river of life in Revelation, and the gathering is the assembly of the redeemed in heaven. It became a beloved funeral and revival hymn in America.

Author: Darlene Zschech
Story: Darlene Zschech, worship leader at Hillsong Church in Sydney, Australia, wrote this song in 1993. It spread rapidly through churches worldwide and became one of the most-sung modern worship songs of its generation, carrying a simple call to praise the Lord of all creation.

Author: Joseph Mohr
Story: Joseph Mohr wrote the German poem Stille Nacht in 1816, and on Christmas Eve 1818 he asked Franz Xaver Gruber, schoolmaster and organist at nearby Arnsdorf, to compose a melody for it for that night's service at St Nicholas Church in Oberndorf, Austria. Mohr sang tenor and Gruber sang bass, with guitar accompaniment, at the first performance. Later romantic stories about a broken organ are not supported by Gruber's own 1854 account, which simply records that Mohr handed him the poem to set to music.

Author: Charles Wesley
Story: Charles Wesley first published this hymn in Hymns and Sacred Poems in 1749 under the title The Whole Armour of God, expanding Paul's exhortation in Ephesians 6 into verse. It was written while the Wesleys faced physical opposition to their preaching, and it became known as a call to spiritual battle. The tune DIADEMATA is its most familiar modern setting.

Author: Keith Getty and Stuart Townend
Story: Keith Getty and Stuart Townend wrote this modern hymn in 2005 as a hymn for the preaching of the Word, asking God to speak through Scripture and shape his people by it. It appeared in the New Irish Hymns series and quickly became a standard opening hymn for services built around Bible teaching.

Hymn: Stand Up, Stand Up for Jesus
Author: George Duffield Jr.
Story: George Duffield Jr. wrote this hymn in 1858 following the death of his friend and fellow minister Dudley Tyng, whose dying exhortation to stand for Christ inspired it. It was first sung at a Young Men's Christian Association meeting in Philadelphia. George Webb's tune Webb, composed earlier in the century, became its standard setting, and the hymn became a rallying song for Christian courage.

Author: William W. Walford
Story: William Walford, an English preacher, is credited with this hymn, which was first published in the New York Observer in 1845. William Bradbury later composed the tune Sweet Hour for it in 1861. The hymn presents prayer as the believer's regular refuge in trouble and as the place where burdens are carried to God.

Author: Samuel John Stone
Story: Samuel John Stone wrote this hymn in 1866 during controversy in the Church of England over the authority of Scripture, as part of a set of hymns on the Apostles' Creed. Samuel Sebastian Wesley composed the tune Aurelia for it in 1864, before the text was written. The hymn confesses one church founded on Christ, united across divisions and sustained through trial.

Author: John of Damascus
Story: John of Damascus, an eighth-century monk and theologian, wrote the Greek Easter canon from which this hymn is drawn, celebrating Christ's rising as the Passover from death to life. John Mason Neale translated it into English in the nineteenth century. It is sung on Easter as a call to rejoice in the empty tomb.

Hymn: The Day Thou Gavest, Lord, Is Ended
Author: John Ellerton
Story: John Ellerton wrote this evening hymn in 1870 for a missionary service, and it was first published in a collection for a choral festival. Clement Scholefield composed the tune St Clement for it in 1874. As evening falls in one land and dawn breaks in another, the hymn pictures unceasing praise circling the earth, and it is widely sung at evening services and at the close of the day.

Author: Thomas Olivers
Story: Thomas Olivers, a follower of John Wesley, wrote this hymn after hearing the Jewish Yigdal sung by cantor Meyer Lyon at the Great Synagogue in London in 1770, and it was first published in 1772. It is a Christian adaptation of the Yigdal, praising the God of Abraham as the eternal King, and its tune LEONI is named for the cantor. The tradition that the melody dates to Solomon's Temple is not established and is not relied on here.

Author: Keith Getty and Stuart Townend
Story: Keith Getty and Stuart Townend wrote this hymn in 2005, tracing the meaning of the crucifixion from Christ's suffering to the believer's forgiveness and new life. Written in the same modern-hymn project as In Christ Alone, it confesses the cross as both the place of shame and the source of salvation.

Hymn: There Is a Fountain Filled with Blood
Author: William Cowper
Story: William Cowper's hymn was first published in 1772 in Richard Conyers's Collection of Psalms and Hymns and republished in the Olney Hymns of 1779. Based on Zechariah 13:1, it presents the blood of Christ as a fountain that cleanses sinners, including the dying thief beside Jesus. It is commonly sung to the American folk tune CLEANSING FOUNTAIN.

Author: Keith Getty and Kristyn Getty
Story: Keith and Kristyn Getty wrote this hymn in 2002, and it appeared on their album In Christ Alone. It pictures the worship of heaven, where the Lamb becomes the Shepherd King, tears are wiped away, and the redeemed sing before God's throne.

Hymn: 'Tis So Sweet to Trust in Jesus
Author: Louisa M. R. Stead
Story: Louisa Stead wrote this hymn in 1882 during a season of hardship following her husband's death, when she and her young daughter faced poverty. William James Kirkpatrick composed the tune Trust in Jesus for it the same year. The hymn testifies to simple, daily trust in Christ through sorrow and uncertainty, and it has remained a standard gospel song of assurance.

Author: Fanny J. Crosby
Story: Fanny Crosby wrote this gospel song with a tune by William Howard Doane, and it was first published in 1875 in Lowry and Doane's collection Brightest and Best, under the title Praise for Redemption. Ira Sankey introduced it in Britain during the Moody campaigns of 1873-1874, where it became popular long before it was widely sung in the United States. Its wider American use followed its revival at the 1954 Billy Graham crusade in London.

Author: Helen H. Lemmel
Story: Helen Lemmel, an English hymnwriter who was blind herself, wrote this hymn in 1922 after reading a missionary tract urging readers to turn their eyes upon Jesus. It became widely used in evangelistic meetings, including the Billy Graham crusades, where its call to look to Christ above earthly troubles struck a broad chord.

Author: Eugene M. Bartlett
Story: Eugene Bartlett, a gospel songwriter and music publisher, wrote this song in 1939 near the end of his life. It tells of redemption from sin and the believer's victory through Christ, and it became a standard of gospel singing, still sung at revivals and funerals generations later.

Author: Philipp Nicolai
Hymn: Wake, Awake, for Night Is Flying
Story: Philipp Nicolai, a Lutheran pastor, wrote this hymn in 1599 during a plague outbreak in Unna, Germany, where he buried many of his parishioners. Cast as the parable of the wise virgins awaiting the bridegroom, it looks to Christ's return and the wedding feast of the Lamb. It is often called the king of chorales and is sung in Advent and at the end of the church year.

Author: Brooke Ligertwood and Ben Fielding
Story: Brooke Ligertwood and Ben Fielding of Hillsong Worship wrote this song in 2016, releasing it on the album let there be light. It celebrates the name of Jesus above every other name, from incarnation to resurrection, and won the 2018 Grammy Award for Best Contemporary Christian Music Performance/Song.

Author: Philip P. Bliss
Story: Philip Bliss wrote both words and tune of this gospel song in 1874, and it became a favourite in evangelistic meetings after he and his wife sang it as a duet during a campaign in New Haven, Connecticut. Bliss, a close associate of Dwight Moody, wrote many of the earliest American gospel songs in the brief period from 1864 until his death in 1876. The song invites hearers to attend to the words of Scripture as words of life.

Author: Jonny Robinson, Rich Thompson and Michael Farren
Hymn: Yet Not I But Through Christ in Me
Story: Jonny Robinson, Rich Thompson, and Michael Farren wrote this hymn for CityAlight, a church music ministry in Sydney, Australia, releasing it in 2018. Built on Paul's words in Galatians 2, it traces the Christian life from the gift of faith to final rest, confessing that every good is through Christ, not self.
